title: Women With Type 2 Diabetes Face Higher Mental Health Risk Than Men, UK Study Finds
excerpt: A study of nearly 29,000 UK patients reveals that women are 53% more likely to develop mental health conditions after a type 2 diabetes diagnosis, while men face higher cardiovascular and kidney risks.
body:
• Women with type 2 diabetes are 53% more likely than men to develop mental health conditions such as depression and anxiety after diagnosis, a UK study of nearly 29,000 patients found.
  • Men face higher rates of cardiovascular disease (8.4% vs 5.3%) and end-stage renal disease following a type 2 diabetes diagnosis.
  • Researchers recommend routine psychological screening for younger women and earlier cardiovascular monitoring for men with type 2 diabetes.
  • With 536.6 million people affected globally — projected to reach 700 million by 2045 — sex-specific care strategies could improve long-term outcomes.

Women diagnosed with type 2 diabetes are significantly more likely to develop mental health conditions in the years following their diagnosis, while men face higher rates of cardiovascular and kidney complications, according to a study published on August 25 in the journal PLOS Medicine.

The research, led by Fabiola Eto at Queen Mary University of London's Wolfson Institute of Population Health, examined anonymised health records from 28,720 men and women in the United Kingdom who developed type 2 diabetes between 2010 and 2020.

Sharp Divergence in Post-Diagnosis Health Trajectories

Men made up 62% of the study cohort, with a median age of 54 at diagnosis. Women were on average older when diagnosed. In the years that followed, 39% of all participants experienced at least one significant health event — but the nature and timing of those events split sharply along sex lines.

Women were more likely to develop mental health conditions after their diabetes diagnosis, at a rate of 8.1% compared to 5.3% for men. Women who developed both type 2 diabetes and a mental health condition also faced a higher risk of premature death.

Men, meanwhile, showed higher rates of cardiovascular disease (8.4% vs 5.3%), end-stage renal disease, and hypertension (21.1% vs 20.2%). The researchers noted that women used more health services and long-term prescriptions than men on average, which may partly account for the higher diagnosis rates of mental health conditions.

"Our research revealed not just which complications show up, but how this wasn't the same story for men and women. Knowing roughly when a complication is likely to happen — and for whom — could provide insights into preventing it."

— Fabiola Eto, Lead Author, Queen Mary University of London

A Call for Sex-Specific Diabetes Care

The study's authors noted that younger women with type 2 diabetes were developing mental health complications "earlier and more often than we expected." They recommend integrating routine psychological screening into standard diabetes care, particularly for younger female patients.

For men, the findings point to the need for earlier and more aggressive monitoring of cardiovascular and kidney health following a type 2 diabetes diagnosis. Current UK guidelines lack sex-specific prevention strategies for type 2 diabetes complications — a gap the researchers say their findings should help address.

Why This Matters for South Asian Communities

Type 2 diabetes is disproportionately prevalent among South Asian populations, with studies consistently showing earlier onset and higher complication rates compared to European populations. The International Diabetes Federation estimates that 536.6 million people between ages 20 and 79 — roughly 10.5% of the global population — currently live with the condition, a figure projected to climb to 700 million by 2045.

For the Indian diaspora, the study's sex-specific findings carry particular weight. South Asian women already face cultural and systemic barriers to mental health care, and the added psychological burden of a diabetes diagnosis underscores the need for proactive screening and support in communities where the condition is common.

What's Next

The researchers acknowledged that their study was observational and based on UK clinical records, which may not fully capture the experiences of other populations. They called for further research across diverse ethnic groups and healthcare systems to validate the sex-specific patterns they identified. The study also highlights the need for clinical trials testing targeted interventions — such as integrated mental health support for women and early cardiovascular screening protocols for men — within diabetes care pathways.
